title: What is Operating Cash Flow?
subtitle: Real cash from operations - how it differs from Net Income
openingQuestion: OCF = Net Income + D&A − ΔNWC. Why is D&A added back?
openingOptions: Because D&A needs to be reinvested
Because D&A is a non-cash expense - already subtracted from NI but no real cash went out
explanation: Operating cash flow is the real cash the business generates, and the common way to calculate it starts from net profit and adjusts for two groups. The first is non-cash expenses like depreciation and provisions, which get added back. The second is the change in working capital: rising inventory and receivables mean cash is being tied up, so they get subtracted. The final number is far harder to distort than profit.

diagram.label: Add back depreciation and other non-cash items
Subtract the increase in working capital
That gives operating cash flow - real cash from the business

realWorldExample.description: Vinamilk has high Net Income and significant D&A from its dairy plants. When calculating OCF, D&A is added back to Net Income, along with adjustments for changes in receivables and inventory - the result is that Vinamilk's OCF is usually higher than its Net Income, reflecting good earnings quality and efficient working-capital management.

quiz.question: What does it usually suggest when OCF is much higher than Net Income?
options: The business is recognising revenue too early
Large depreciation combined with well-managed working capital
The business just took on a large amount of new debt during the period
Accounting profit is being understated
quiz.explanation: OCF > NI is usually a good sign: large D&A (a heavy asset base), efficient WC management, few hard-to-collect receivables. The business generates more real cash than accounting profit.

quiz.question: A company has very large D&A, but Operating Cash Flow is only slightly higher than Net Income (not proportional to D&A). What should this prompt you to check?
options: Net Income for the period is being significantly understated
The company recorded depreciation incorrectly under accounting standards
Another item, like receivables or inventory, is eating into it
Interest expense was added back into OCF incorrectly
quiz.explanation: OCF = Net Income + D&A − ΔNWC (working capital increase). If D&A is large but OCF only nudges up over NI, it's very likely ΔNWC (e.g. AR or Inventory rising sharply) is cancelling out most of the benefit from adding back D&A - a signal worth watching closely.

quiz.question: Why is depreciation added back when calculating Operating Cash Flow?
options: Because accounting rules require every expense to be added back
Because depreciation is money the company gets back from the tax authority each year
Because depreciation is recorded under investing, not operating
Because it was subtracted from profit but no real cash actually went out
quiz.explanation: The cash was spent years earlier, when the asset was purchased. Depreciation is just a way of spreading that spending across the years of use - it lowers profit without touching the bank account, so it must be added back.

quiz.question: Receivables rise by 50 billion during the period. How does this affect Operating Cash Flow?
options: It lowers OCF by exactly 50 billion - revenue was recognised but the cash hasn't come in yet
It raises OCF by 50 billion, since receivables are an asset of the company
No effect, since receivables only sit on the balance sheet
It lowers OCF by 50 billion and also lowers the corresponding recognised revenue
quiz.explanation: The revenue has already hit the P&L but the cash is still with the customer. A ballooning working capital is literally your money stuck out there - and that's why fast-growing companies often run short of cash.

quiz.question: A company collects cash immediately on sales but pays suppliers slowly. What's the effect on working capital?
options: It ties up cash, since the company must fund all of its inventory purchases upfront
It frees up cash - this is exactly the negative working capital model of retail
No effect, since these two items fully cancel each other out
It ties up cash short-term but frees it up once the debt is paid off
quiz.explanation: Collecting first and paying later means suppliers are financing your working capital for free. This is the advantage of supermarkets and subscription models - and why negative working capital is a strength, not a risk, in those industries.

quiz.question: OCF consistently runs much higher than Net Income at an infrastructure company. What is the most plausible reason?
options: The company took on a lot of new debt, raising operating cash flow
The company is recognising revenue earlier than actual delivery
Large depreciation from fixed assets, lowering profit without costing cash
Interest expense was added back into operating cash flow
quiz.explanation: Plants, pipelines, and power stations generate enormous depreciation every year. Profit looks thin as a result while cash keeps coming in steadily - which is why infrastructure is often valued on EBITDA or cash flow rather than P/E.

keyTakeaways: OCF = real cash from the business, adjusted from Net Income
D&A is added back as non-cash; a rising WC is subtracted as it consumes cash
OCF sustainably above NI signals high earnings quality

practicePrompt.question: A company has Net Income of 150 billion, depreciation (D&A) of 60 billion (a non-cash cost), and working capital that grew by 40 billion (from rising inventory and receivables). What is this company's OCF?
options: OCF = 150 billion, exactly equal to Net Income, since that is the company's official profit figure
OCF = 170 billion: Net Income 150 + D&A 60 (non-cash, so added back) - working capital 40 (cash used)
OCF = 210 billion, since you only need to add back depreciation without subtracting the working-capital increase
OCF = 90 billion, since both depreciation and the working-capital increase must be subtracted from Net Income
practicePrompt.explanation: OCF = real cash from the business, adjusted from Net Income: D&A is added back since it's a non-cash cost (150+60=210), and the working-capital increase is subtracted since it consumes real cash (210-40=170 billion). OCF sustainably exceeding NI is a sign of good earnings quality.

summary.keyIdea: OCF = real cash from the business, adjusted from Net Income
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: D&A is added back as non-cash; a rising WC is subtracted as it consumes cash

application.title: Cross-check a company's Net Income and OCF
application.message: Take the Net Income and OCF of the same company for the same period, and see where the gap comes from by looking at the D&A adjustment and the working-capital change on the Cash Flow Statement.
application.secondary: If OCF sustainably exceeds Net Income across several years, that's usually a good sign.

sections.text: Net Income is an accounting number, shaped by non-cash recognition rules. Operating Cash Flow (OCF) answers a more practical question: how much cash did the core business actually generate during the period?
The formula: from Net Income to OCF

The most common approach - the indirect method - starts from Net Income and adjusts for non-cash items: OCF = Net Income + D&A − ΔNWC (change in net working capital). D&A (Depreciation & Amortization) is an expense already subtracted from Net Income on the P&L but which cost no cash this period - because the cash was already spent back when the asset was purchased. That's why D&A has to be added back.

ΔNWC (change in net working capital) reflects cash being 'tied up' or 'freed' by operations: if receivables (AR) and inventory rise, cash is being tied up (subtracted from OCF); if payables (AP) rise, the company is using supplier funding - cash is kept longer, raising OCF.
What does OCF say about earnings quality?

Comparing OCF with Net Income across several years lets an investor judge 'earnings quality'. If OCF consistently runs well below Net Income, that's a warning sign: the company might be recognising revenue too early, letting receivables balloon, or holding unsellable inventory. Conversely, OCF sustainably exceeding Net Income across several years is a sign of a healthy business managing its working capital well.

items: D&A: a non-cash cost, added back to Net Income
Rising AR and Inventory: cash tied up, subtracted from OCF
Rising AP: the company uses supplier funding, added to OCF
OCF sustainably above NI over several years: a sign of high earnings quality

sections.label: Compare OCF with NI - don't look at just one number
sections.text: A company with beautifully growing Net Income but flat or falling OCF for several quarters running is a signal worth investigating closely - profit may well be 'painted' through early revenue recognition or delayed expense recognition.

concepts.def: A non-cash cost that spreads the value of fixed/intangible assets over their useful life.
The gap between current operating assets and current operating liabilities (AR + Inventory − AP).
How well Net Income is backed by real cash flow rather than just accounting entries.

lines: OCF is the 'real cash' picture of a business's operations, unlike Net Income, which is shaped by accrual accounting.
Comparing OCF and Net Income over time is one of the fastest ways to judge a business's earnings quality.
